title: Represent the mathematics
artifact: A versioned statement and argument record

slides.title: A plausible claim with a missing hypothesis
slides.body:
Every continuous real-valued function on (0, 1) attains a maximum.

f(x) = x is a counterexample.
slides.script: Consider the sentence on the screen. It sounds like a familiar theorem. Before we design an agent, decide whether it is true. For f(x) = x, every point in the open interval has a larger point still inside the interval. There is no maximum. The familiar extreme value theorem requires a compact domain. Our first design problem is therefore very concrete: how do we prevent a familiar-looking conclusion from hiding a changed hypothesis? A stronger model may make this mistake less often. We still need a representation that lets us detect it and identify exactly which statement was considered.

slides.title: Statements and arguments are separate objects
slides.body:
Statement: domain, quantifiers, assumptions, conclusion
Argument: premises, inference, unresolved obligations
Review: the exact version examined
slides.script: A statement records what is claimed. An argument records a proposed reason to believe it. Those are different objects because a true statement can have a bad argument, and several arguments can support the same statement. Write the domain and conclusion explicitly. Give the argument its own identifier and list its premises. A review then refers to an exact version of this content. If we change the open interval to the closed interval, we have changed the mathematical task. We should preserve that revision rather than silently treating the earlier review as approval of the new record. A schema checks that fields exist. It does not check that the mathematics inside them is correct.

slides.title: Laboratory: a well-formed false claim
slides.body:
Run the false-mathematics fixture.
Explain why its software test passes.
Repair the mathematical statement explicitly.
slides.script: We will now run a test whose purpose is to demonstrate a limitation. The workbench can mark this false statement usable when supplied with a stipulated review. That behavior exposes its trust boundary: it manages evidence records but does not decide mathematical truth. Your task is to write the counterexample, revise the domain explicitly, and attach a new argument to the revised statement. Keep the rejected version. At the end, another person should be able to reconstruct both the mistake and the repair without guessing what the system originally meant.

demo: In files/math-reasoning-lab, run: python -B -m unittest test_workbench.WorkbenchTests.test_wrong_math_can_pass_policy -v. Open the test and point to the stipulated informal review. Write f(x)=x on (0,1), then revise the domain to [0,1] in a separate statement record.
pause: Which checks can a record schema perform, and which require mathematical evidence?
answer: A schema can require a domain, premises, and a version identifier. It cannot establish the extreme value theorem or validate its application merely from those fields.
exercise: Submit the false statement, its counterexample, the revised statement, and a new argument record. Explain why changing the domain changes the task.

title: Plan and search
artifact: A dependency plan with joint premises and alternative routes

slides.title: A circular plan supplies no starting point
slides.body:
Proposed route 1: B implies A
Proposed route 2: A implies B

Neither route supplies a proof of A or B.
slides.script: Suppose one task promises to prove A using B, while another promises to prove B using A. Both tasks may be well written. Both implications may even be correct. Still, we have no proof of either statement without an independent starting point. This is the difference between an execution cycle and a grounded mathematical argument. Retrying the tasks or adding another worker does not manufacture the missing premise. In a genuine induction, a base case and a decreasing parameter supply the structure that this circular plan lacks.

slides.title: Joint premises and alternative arguments
slides.body:
One argument may need P and Q.
A different argument may establish the same target.

Search chooses an action. Evidence justifies a conclusion.
slides.script: Represent an argument as requiring all of its premises. Represent different arguments for the same target as alternatives. If one route fails, the other may remain useful. This distinction also helps choose the next action. A short source check may unblock a route; a counterexample probe may eliminate it. The search policy decides where to spend time, but its choice is not itself a mathematical justification. We can improve that policy as models improve without changing what it means for the premises of an argument to be established.

slides.title: Laboratory: a cycle and an independent base
slides.body:
Run the unsupported-cycle fixture.
Add an independent proof of A.
Observe which conclusions become usable.
slides.script: The fixture first creates the two circular implications and attaches stipulated reviews. The closure remains empty. It then adds an independent argument for A. Now B can follow through the reviewed implication. Inspect this change rather than merely noticing a green test result. For your own plan, give one target two routes and put a strict budget on exploratory actions. Record the reason for each action and what it changed. A failed route that rules out a serious possibility can be useful progress, provided we record its actual scope.

demo: Run: python -B -m unittest test_workbench.WorkbenchTests.test_unsupported_cycle_cannot_bootstrap -v. Show the assertions before and after the independent base argument. On a board, draw premises into argument nodes and argument nodes into conclusions.
pause: If both implications have correct proofs, why is the original circular plan still insufficient?
answer: The implications establish conditional statements. They do not establish either antecedent. An independent base or a valid well-founded induction is still required.
exercise: Create one target with two alternative arguments, one of which needs two premises. Execute at most four exploratory actions and report what each action established or ruled out.

title: Use the literature
artifact: A source record and an applicability audit

slides.title: A relevant theorem can still be inapplicable
slides.body:
Source theorem: a continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact domain attains a maximum.

Application: the domain is (0, 1).
slides.script: Finding a relevant theorem is only the beginning of a theorem application. Return to our maximum example. The source theorem is useful and correct, but its compactness hypothesis is not satisfied by the proposed domain. More retrieval results will not repair that mismatch. The research system must distinguish evidence about what a source says from evidence that its hypotheses hold here. Otherwise a strong retrieval engine can produce a confidently cited invalid argument.

slides.title: An applicability record
slides.body:
Exact theorem and source location
Mapping of source objects to current objects
Evidence for each hypothesis
The conclusion that actually transfers
slides.script: For each proposed application, preserve the source version and theorem location. Identify which object in our problem plays each role in the theorem. Then write a row for each hypothesis and attach its justification. A missing row is an open obligation, not an invitation to infer that the author probably intended it. Finally, write the conclusion after substituting our objects. This last step catches applications that prove something nearby but not the target. For an advanced class, repeat the exercise with a vanishing theorem and check the geometric category and positivity assumptions carefully.

slides.title: Workshop: a useful rejected match
slides.body:
Record one applicable theorem.
Preserve one rejected near-match.
Stop when the search budget expires.
slides.script: Open a textbook or paper you already have permission to use. Locate an exact theorem rather than relying on a model's paraphrase. We will prepare one successful application and one near-match that fails a hypothesis. Keeping the rejected match prevents the next search round from repeating the same error. It also documents a possible research direction: perhaps the missing hypothesis can be proved, or perhaps a different theorem is needed. Neither possibility should be recorded as a completed application until the mathematical bridge is supplied.

demo: Open a selected source theorem and record its edition or revision and theorem number. Fill a two-column table: source hypothesis and evidence in this problem. Use the compact-domain example as the first rejected application. This is a manual evidence exercise; the Python lab does not implement retrieval.
pause: What evidence is still missing after we verify that the quotation is accurate?
answer: We still need the object mapping, justification of every hypothesis in the current setting, and confirmation that the instantiated conclusion supports the target.
exercise: Submit a source record, one justified application, and one rejected near-match. Record the search budget and the unresolved hypothesis without inventing a citation.

title: Change the viewpoint
artifact: A transformation contract with an explicit return argument

slides.title: Separate bounds do not give a uniform bound
slides.body:
For every n, there exists C with n ≤ C.

There exists C such that every n satisfies n ≤ C.

The first statement is true. The second is false.
slides.script: A research strategy often replaces a hard problem with simpler ones. That is useful only when we understand how the answers return to the original target. Here each individual natural number has a bound. Solving all of those individual problems does not give one common bound. The witness in the first statement may depend on n. In the second statement it must be chosen before n. This elementary distinction appears in serious arguments about uniform estimates and limiting processes. A large collection of successful local tasks can therefore leave the central research problem unresolved.

slides.title: The return argument is a proof obligation
slides.body:
Original target
Construction and its preconditions
New subproblem
Implication back to the original target
slides.script: A transformation record should tell us what we started with, what construction we performed, and which hypotheses permit that construction. It should then state the new problem and the implication that would return us to the target. Do not hide that implication inside a phrase such as standard reduction. Sometimes the transformation is an equivalence. Sometimes it gives only a sufficient condition. Sometimes we have only a promising analogy. Recording which situation we are in prevents partial success from being reported as completion.

slides.title: Workshop: the missing uniformity bridge
slides.body:
Choose C = n for each individual problem.
Try a proposed common bound C.
Choose n = C + 1.
Locate the failed return implication.
slides.script: Write down the local witness C equals n. Next let a classmate propose a single common bound. Choose its successor and show the failure. The point is not that the calculation is difficult. The point is that we can locate exactly where the proposed transformation loses the target. Your method card should now say that the local problems are solved and the return implication is false in this example. In a research problem, the corresponding bridge may instead remain open. Those statuses must be distinguishable.

demo: Display the two quantifier orders side by side. Ask for a proposed common natural-number bound and choose its successor. Mark the return edge as invalid, while keeping the local witness construction correct. Module 6 formalizes this same example.
pause: Does solving every transformed subproblem prove the original target?
answer: Only if the required return implication has been justified. In this example, independent witnesses do not supply a common witness.
exercise: Write a transformation card for an argument you know. State the preconditions and return implication. Include one variant with an open or invalid bridge and label its status precisely.

title: Review and admit results
artifact: A review bound to an exact argument version

slides.title: A review applies to the argument it examined
slides.body:
Version 1: a fixed chosen section lifts.
Version 2: a different section is chosen.

The old review cannot automatically approve version 2.
slides.script: Imagine that a reviewer checks a lifting argument for a particular section. Later the system changes the section but retains the approval flag. The report may be correct about the old argument and irrelevant to the new one. This is an evidence-management failure even before we debate reviewer quality. We need to bind the review to the content it examined. A version identifier or digest helps detect changes, although a digest alone does not authenticate who performed the review.

slides.title: Status, evidence, and scope
slides.body:
Status: candidate, admitted, withdrawn
Evidence: source check, informal review, formal check
Scope: unconditional or conditional on stated assumptions
slides.script: One verified flag is too ambiguous. Workflow status tells us what the system has done. Evidence kind tells us what checking procedure supports the argument. Scope tells us which assumptions remain. A conditional argument can be useful, but its assumptions must remain visible in downstream conclusions. An informal review and a kernel-checked proof are different kinds of evidence. Neither an impressive reviewer name nor agreement among several models permits us to silently upgrade one kind into another.

slides.title: Laboratory: stale and conditional evidence
slides.body:
Reject a review of an outdated version.
Keep assumptions attached to conclusions.
Require formal evidence and inspect what remains unresolved.
slides.script: Run the stale-review and conditional-scope examples. Then ask the workbench to allow only formal evidence. The fixture's informal reviews no longer satisfy that policy. Notice that the software is enforcing a rule about supplied records; it is not invoking Lean. Your assignment is to write an admission decision that another researcher can audit. It should identify the exact argument, the evidence actually obtained, and the scope of permitted reuse. When the evidence is insufficient, an unresolved result is the correct output.

demo: Run three tests: test_stale_review_rejected, test_assumptions_remain_visible, and test_evidence_types_are_not_interchangeable in test_workbench.WorkbenchTests. Inspect the report fields. Explain that the fixture reviews are stipulated evidence.
pause: Can a conditional argument be admitted without proving its assumption?
answer: Yes, for explicitly conditional use. Its assumption must remain visible and must not silently become an established premise.
exercise: Submit one current review, one rejected stale review, and one conditional conclusion. Specify the evidence policy under which each can be reused.

title: Formalize a proof with Lean
artifact: A checked proof and a statement-alignment report

slides.title: A witness in Lean
slides.body:
theorem pointwiseBound :
    ∀ n : Nat, ∃ C : Nat, n ≤ C := by
  intro n
  exact ⟨n, Nat.le_refl n⟩
slides.script: We now formalize the example from Module 4. Read the statement before reading the proof. Nat fixes the domain, and the quantifiers tell us when the witness may depend on the input. After intro n, our context contains an arbitrary natural number and our goal asks for a bound for that number. The pair supplies the witness n and a proof that n is at most itself. Open the editor's proof state and follow this change one line at a time. The important learning outcome is the relation between the mathematical statement and the remaining obligation, rather than memorizing a tactic.

slides.title: Compilation does not settle admission
slides.body:
Broken proof: type mismatch
sorry: compiles with a placeholder axiom
Extra axiom: compiles using the assumed claim

#print axioms exposes declaration dependencies.
slides.script: Run all three damaged examples. The first tries to use a proof of P where Q is required and fails. The second uses sorry, so compilation can succeed even though the proof is unfinished. The third contains no sorry but assumes the desired conclusion as an axiom. For these fixed examples, inspect the printed axiom dependencies. Our completed elementary proofs need no axioms. Larger developments may deliberately use standard foundations, so the general policy is to state and audit the allowed dependencies, not blindly reject every axiom. The regression script checks these fixtures only. It is not a secure verifier for arbitrary generated code.

slides.title: The intended statement remains part of the task
slides.body:
Compare domains, quantifiers, and assumptions.
Pin the toolchain and library dependencies.
Complete the successor-witness exercise.
Record the exact declaration and validation output.
slides.script: A correct proof of the pointwise statement does not prove a uniform bound. Formal checking therefore needs a companion task: compare the encoded proposition with the intended mathematics. Complete the exercise that uses a successor as a strict upper bound, then reconstruct the proof that there is no largest natural number. Record the exact declarations and their axiom reports. For research mathematics, begin with a small lemma supported by existing library definitions. Formalizing one fragile bridge can be useful, but it does not certify the rest of an informal paper. For unreviewed generated source, use isolation and a suitable stronger validation procedure rather than trusting displayed output alone.

demo: In files/lean-reasoning-lab, run lake build, lake env lean Formalization.lean, and python check.py. In the editor, place the cursor after intro n. Then run each fixtures/*.lean file individually. Use Lean 4.19.0 from lean-toolchain. Open Solutions.lean only after the exercise.
pause: Which successful compilations in the fixtures are unacceptable under the lesson's policy, and why?
answer: Incomplete.lean depends on sorryAx. ExtraAxiom.lean depends on inventedBound. Neither supplies the required proof under our policy. A checked proof of a different proposition would also fail statement alignment.
exercise: Complete Exercises.lean and submit the informal/formal statement comparison, version information, axiom reports, and admission decision.

title: Remember and recover
artifact: A reproducible snapshot and a withdrawal report

slides.title: Losing an argument need not lose the conclusion
slides.body:
Route A supports the target.
Route B independently supports the target.

Withdraw A. Check whether B still applies.
slides.script: Suppose a source audit invalidates one argument. It is tempting to mark the conclusion false, but that does not follow. Another argument may still establish it. Conversely, retaining the conclusion merely because it was once approved is also wrong. We must recompute what the remaining evidence supports. In the section-lifting case, a sufficient vanishing route and a direct obstruction calculation can support the same target. Withdrawing one route need not remove the other.

slides.title: Recovery preserves mathematical state
slides.body:
Keep statements, versions, arguments, and evidence.
Recompute usable conclusions after withdrawal.
Distinguish a timeout from a mathematical obstruction.
slides.script: A saved conversation is not always enough to restore a research state. We need the target, current versions, dependencies, evidence records, and open obligations. Operational failures need separate treatment. A timeout tells us that an execution did not complete within its limit. It does not refute the lemma. A counterexample has mathematical content. A reproducible snapshot should let us recover these distinctions and obtain the same report from the same state. Our teaching implementation assumes one writer and does not provide database transactions or authenticated reviews.

slides.title: Laboratory: withdrawal and replay
slides.body:
Withdraw one alternative route.
Withdraw the remaining support.
Reload a snapshot and compare the report.
Change saved content and detect the mismatch.
slides.script: Run the alternative-route test and inspect the report after each withdrawal. Then run the save-and-reload test. The restored report should agree with the saved one. The final mutation deliberately changes mathematical content and should invalidate the old digest relationship. This demonstrates a useful integrity check, but it is not a security guarantee against a party that can rewrite all records and digests. In your report, separate reproducibility, content integrity, and authentication. They solve related but different problems.

demo: Run test_alternative_survives_then_both_fail and test_save_reload_and_tamper in test_workbench.WorkbenchTests. Inspect the withdrawal reasons and compare the saved and loaded target reports.
pause: What can we conclude when the only currently usable argument is withdrawn?
answer: The target is no longer supported by the available admitted evidence. It is unresolved in this state, not automatically false.
exercise: Save a state with two routes, withdraw each route in turn, and replay the reports. Add a separate simulated timeout and explain why its status differs from a refutation.

title: Coordinate the work
artifact: A comparison of sequential and divided work

slides.title: More workers introduce a coordination problem
slides.body:
Worker A checks source applicability.
Worker B explores a different argument.

Both need the exact target version.
slides.script: This module is optional. A good mathematical reasoning system does not require multiple agents. Division of work becomes useful when tasks can proceed independently or require different evidence. One worker might audit a source while another explores a direct proof. But both must know the exact target and assumptions. If the target changes while a worker is running, its eventual report must be checked against the current version before reuse. More workers can increase useful coverage, duplicated effort, or both.

slides.title: Reports carry evidence rather than votes
slides.body:
Task identifier and target version
Evidence produced and remaining obligations
Dependencies and resource use
Disagreements preserved for review
slides.script: A report should say what task was attempted, what evidence it produced, and what remains unresolved. Agreement among workers is not a proof rule. They may share a source error or repeat the same invalid inference. When reports disagree, preserve the underlying arguments so that the disagreement can be investigated. Start with scripted workers if the purpose is to test the protocol. Model capability can then change without changing the requirement that each report refer to an identifiable mathematical task.

slides.title: Workshop: does the extra worker help?
slides.body:
Fix the total budget.
Compare sequential and divided execution.
Count useful evidence and duplicated work.
Inject one delayed report for an old version.
slides.script: Run the same small task sequentially and with divided responsibilities. Fix a total effort budget rather than giving the multi-worker system twice the resources and calling the comparison fair. Record elapsed time, total cost or calls, accepted evidence, and repeated work. Then deliver a report for an outdated target and verify that the merge procedure does not silently accept it. If the extra worker brings no useful benefit for this task, simplify the architecture. That conclusion is a successful design result.

demo: Use two manually prepared reports or scripted workers. Assign a source audit and an alternative-proof task. Change the target version before delivering one report. Record whether the merge accepts, rejects, or requests a new review. No concurrent worker implementation is supplied by the Python lab.
pause: Why is agreement between two agents weaker than two independent mathematical justifications?
answer: Agreement may repeat shared errors and does not expose the inference. Independent justifications must each supply applicable premises and a valid argument.
exercise: Submit a budget-matched sequential/divided comparison, a stale-report example, and a decision about whether the extra worker is worthwhile for this task.

title: Evaluate and assemble
artifact: An evaluated research episode with a simpler baseline

slides.title: Rejecting everything is not success
slides.body:
Valid proof: should remain usable.
Missing hypothesis: should be caught.
Invalid return argument: should remain unresolved.

Report false acceptance and false rejection separately.
slides.script: A system that rejects every argument can look safe on a collection containing only bad proofs. It is not useful for research. Our evaluation therefore needs valid controls as well as damaged variants. Start with a short proof you understand. Remove a necessary hypothesis in one variant and break a return implication in another. Measure whether the system preserves the valid case and diagnoses the damaged ones. A correct partial result can be useful, but it must not be counted as a completed proof of the original target.

slides.title: Three evaluation questions
slides.body:
Does the software implement its stated rules?
Does the evidence support the mathematical claim?
Does the system help this research task at acceptable cost?
slides.script: These questions require different evidence. Unit tests can check version handling and withdrawal behavior. They cannot establish every mathematical assertion placed in a record. Mathematical review or suitable formal checking addresses proof content. Research usefulness asks whether the architecture improves progress relative to a simpler baseline, taking cost and maintenance into account. Do not combine these into one impressive score that hides which property was actually tested. Report the failures and the task conditions under which the result was obtained.

slides.title: The capstone research episode
slides.body:
One known proof and two damaged variants
Versioned records and one transformation
Reproducible checks and an honest failure report
A justified decision to keep or remove each mechanism
slides.script: For the capstone, assemble the artifacts from the earlier modules around one mathematical problem. Include the original target, source applications, proposed arguments, reviews, and remaining obligations. Compare against a simpler workflow. Explain which component caught a real failure or saved useful work, and which component did not justify its cost. As AI improves, rerun this evaluation and replace mechanisms that no longer help. What persists is the discipline of defining the task, preserving evidence, and evaluating actual mathematical progress. We do not need a prediction that any particular activity will remain exclusively human in order to teach those requirements.

demo: Run python -B -m unittest discover -s files/math-reasoning-lab -p test_workbench.py -v from the repository root. Explain what the eight tests cover. Then evaluate the chosen proof and two damaged variants separately; do not count the fixture suite as a mathematical benchmark.
pause: What evidence would justify removing a component from the system?
answer: A task-relevant comparison shows no useful benefit, or the benefit does not justify its resource and maintenance costs. Preserve necessary correctness requirements while simplifying their implementation.
exercise: Submit the complete episode, valid and damaged cases, baseline comparison, resource record, and one documented failure. State which conclusions are proved, conditional, or unresolved.
